page_hint: Ch 6 §6, Architecture Consequence
quoted_clause: P/D disaggregation (Splitwise/DistServe/Mooncake) is the remedy at scale
observed: The claim that P/D disaggregation 'is the remedy at scale' is too strong. It implies it's THE remedy, not A remedy. P/D disaggregation adds communication overhead (KV transfer), operational complexity (two pools), and potential for imbalance.
evidence: The text doesn't discuss the trade-offs of P/D disaggregation. The claim is labeled [S4][1P][FACT] but is an architectural interpretation, not a first-party fact.
root_cause: The claim is presented as a universal solution without acknowledging trade-offs or conditions under which it may not help.
correction: Change 'is the remedy at scale' to 'can be a remedy at scale' or 'is one remedy at scale,' and briefly note the trade-offs (KV transfer overhead, operational complexity, potential imbalance).
acceptance_test: After correction, the claim should be scoped and the trade-offs should be acknowledged.

page_hint: Appendix A §1 (DeepSeek-V4), 'What this means for the architect'
quoted_clause: DeepSeek shows the *constant factor itself* can be cut ~10–14× across the V4 variants (the ~14× end is V4-Flash's ~7%-of-V3.2 single-token KV, §5) through attention re-architecture alone — the parameter count is unchanged, so the saving is architectural, not a smaller model.
observed: As written, 'the parameter count is unchanged' is false or unresolvable. V4-Pro is 1.6 T total and V4-Flash is 284 B total, so the parameter count is not unchanged across the variants the sentence is about; and the appendix never states V3.2's parameter count, so the reader cannot check 'unchanged' against the reference model. The intended claim is that the KV/FLOP constant changed without the model being shrunk.
evidence: §1: 'V4-Pro is 1.6 T total / 49 B activated, V4-Flash 284 B / 13 B activated'. No V3.2 parameter count appears anywhere in the chunk.
root_cause: The sentence was written to make a point about the attention scheme and left ambiguous about which pair of models 'unchanged' refers to.
correction: Rewrite: 'the saving comes from the attention scheme rather than from a smaller model — the parameter count is not what changed.' If the claim is meant relative to V3.2, state V3.2's parameter count and cite it.
acceptance_test: The sentence is true under every reading a reader can construct from the appendix's own numbers, or it names the reference model and its parameter count.

page_hint: Ch 7, §5 Common Mistakes, bullet 4 (KV quantization per bit width)
quoted_clause: FP8 KV ≈50% of FP16 (raw byte-halving) is what serving stacks realize today
observed: The phrase 'is what serving stacks realize today' is a universal present-tense claim about all current serving stacks. The text itself immediately qualifies this in §4 point 4: 'Do not generalize a fixed ratio to all FP8-KV deployments: the realized per-token footprint depends on the engine version, cache-block layout, scale/offset metadata, allocator rounding, and the accounting boundary.' The Common Mistakes bullet slightly overstates relative to the text's own qualification.
evidence: §4 point 4 explicitly warns against generalizing the 50% ratio. The Common Mistakes bullet uses 'is what serving stacks realize today' without the same hedging.
root_cause: The Common Mistakes section compresses the qualified statement into a shorter form, losing the 'raw byte-halving, before metadata' scope.
correction: Change to: 'FP8 KV ≈50% of FP16 (raw byte-halving, before block/scale metadata) is the first-order figure serving stacks use today' or add '(raw payload; see §4.4 for the full accounting caveat).'
acceptance_test: The bullet no longer implies that every serving stack's observed resident memory is exactly 50% of FP16; it identifies the raw byte-halving as the first-order planning figure.

page_hint: Ch 7, §4 Measurement, point 1 (KV per-token formula introduction)
quoted_clause: The per-token KV footprint of a fully-cached (MHA) attention head is
observed: The word 'head' is incorrect. The formula that follows (2 × n_layers × d_hidden × bytes-per-value) computes the total per-token KV for the entire model across all layers, not for a single attention head. The parenthetical '(one key and one value per layer, each d_hidden wide)' confirms the formula spans all layers. A single head's per-token KV would be 2 × d_head × bytes (no layer count).
evidence: Formula: 2 × 80 × 8192 × 2 = 2,621,440 B. This is the whole-model value (all 80 layers). Per-head would be 2 × 8192/64 × 2 = 512 B (for 64 heads of 128 dim each). The text's own worked example confirms the 2.62 MB/token figure is the model total.
root_cause: Typo or editing artifact: 'head' should be 'model' (or 'transformer').
correction: Change to: 'The per-token KV footprint of a fully-cached (MHA) model is' or 'The per-token KV footprint for a fully-cached (MHA) transformer is'.
acceptance_test: The sentence introduces a formula whose result (2.62 MB/token) matches the whole-model KV, not a per-head value. A reader should not be able to interpret the formula as per-head.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph following the host-count table; compare Ch 8 §1 'Three different bounds' callout
quoted_clause: This rough sizing illustrates that prefill is FLOP-bound at this scale — the compute requirement is the primary constraint, and memory bandwidth (HBM at 3.35 TB/s per H100) is sufficient to keep the compute fed if the kernel is efficient.
observed: The chapter's own screen table, printed a few lines earlier, shows the opposite ordering under the linear-only case: the KV-residency/Little's-Law screen gives 21 hosts at peak while the compute screen gives 19 hosts under case (i) and 21 under case (iii). The compute screen binds only under case (ii) (22 hosts). So 'the compute requirement is the primary constraint' is true only under the conservative FLOP-counting case, and the sentence is stated unconditionally. The §1 callout's claim that the canonical workload 'illustrates all three without overlap' is in the same tension.
evidence: Ch 8 §3: 'the capacity floor is the max of the named screens — 21 hosts under case (i), 22 under case (ii)'; the KV screen is ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts.
root_cause: A summary sentence written from the roofline argument (prefill is compute-bound) without reconciling it against the fleet screens derived in the same section.
correction: Rewrite: 'This sizing illustrates that prefill is FLOP-bound at this scale — its arithmetic intensity (~9,200 FLOP/byte) is far above the ridge, so HBM bandwidth is sufficient to keep the compute fed. Whether prefill *compute* or KV *residency* is the binding fleet constraint is decided by the screens above: KV residency binds under cases (i) and (iii), compute under case (ii).' Amend the §1 callout's 'without overlap' to 'with the binding constraint depending on the FLOP-counting case'.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 8 asserts that compute is the primary fleet constraint without naming the FLOP-counting case under which that holds.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3 'Scope' note; Ch 6 §8 mini-case; Ch 5 §3(b)
quoted_clause: Scope. "1 host with 8×H100" here is a **per-host / per-request** feasibility container (does one host meet one request's latency and memory SLO). It is **not** a claim that one host absorbs the 40 rps peak arrival rate
observed: The Scope note disclaims only the peak rate. The canonical workload's *average* rate is ~10 rps, and the chapter's own arithmetic shows one host is insufficient there too: 92,000 prefill tokens/s ÷ 19,800 tokens/s per host ≈ 4.6 → ~5 hosts, and Ch 17's KV-residency screen at 10 rps (λ·W = 10 × 8.6 = 86 in-flight; 86/17 ≈ 5.1 → 6 hosts) agrees. Ch 6's mini-case nevertheless says 'The architecture is memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point', and Ch 5's worked example treats the single 8×H100 host as the serving configuration for the workload. The canonical scenario therefore reads as 'one host serves the workload' in at least three places while the book's own screens say five to six hosts at the average rate.
evidence: Ch 8 §3: 'n_hosts = 92,000/19,800 ≈ 4.6 → ~5 hosts'. Ch 8 §3 Scope note addresses only the 40 rps peak. Ch 6 §8: 'memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point'.
root_cause: The canonical scenario's '1 host' was reinterpreted locally as a per-request container in Ch 8 but never re-labelled in Ch 4's table or in the chapters that reuse it, so the ambiguity propagates.
correction: Extend the Scope note to the average rate ('one host does not absorb the 10 rps average either: the prefill screen alone needs ~5 hosts'), and re-label the canonical row in Ch 4 Table 4-2 as 'per-request feasibility container (1 host of 8×H100); fleet sizing in Ch 17'. Adjust Ch 6's mini-case wording so 'sane at the 10 rps design point' refers to the per-host resource envelope, not to the fleet.
acceptance_test: A reader who reads only Ch 4's canonical table and Ch 6's mini-case cannot conclude that a single 8×H100 host serves the canonical workload at 10 rps.

page_hint: Ch 8 §5 Common Mistakes, second bullet; compare Ch 8 §3 and Ch 6 §3
quoted_clause: Treating prefill and decode as having the same FLOP/byte profile. Prefill reads the full context once and is FLOP-bound; decode re-reads weights per token and is memory-bound.
observed: The Common Mistakes section states the two regimes unconditionally, which is the exact universal framing the rest of the book carefully avoids. Ch 8 §3 qualifies prefill as 'compute-bound at the canonical long-prompt operating point' and decode as 'memory-bound at low batch', and Ch 6 §3 adds '(This is an operating-point property, not an identity: at high batch decode climbs the intensity slope and can become compute-bound.)' The summary bullet drops both qualifiers, and a reader who consults only the Common Mistakes list will carry the universal version.
evidence: Ch 8 §3: 'at batch=32 the effective intensity is ~32 FLOP/byte, still ~9× below the 295 ridge'; 'decode stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size' only after the KV term is included; Ch 6 §3: 'the same hardware, the same model — the boundary flips between prefill and decode'.
root_cause: The Common Mistakes bullets were written as slogans rather than as compressed versions of the chapter's qualified findings.
correction: Rewrite: 'Treating prefill and decode as having the same FLOP/byte profile. At the canonical operating point prefill is compute-bound (intensity ~9,200 FLOP/byte, far above the ~295 ridge) and low-batch decode is bandwidth-bound (~1 FLOP/byte) — but both are operating-point properties: decode's intensity rises with batch, and prefill's falls as context shortens.'
acceptance_test: Every regime statement in Ch 8's Common Mistakes carries the same operating-point qualifier as the corresponding statement in §3.

page_hint: Ch 8 §4 Measurement, item 3
quoted_clause: GB200: higher on both terms (dense BF16 peak 4,500 TFLOPS = 2× B200's 2,250, over 16 TB/s HBM3e → 4,500 ÷ 16 ≈ 281 FLOP/byte, just below H100's ~295 — its 4.8× bandwidth advantage slightly outpaces its 4.5× compute advantage)
observed: The ridge value (281 FLOP/byte) is correct, but the granularity is unstated: 4,500 TFLOPS and 16 TB/s are both *per GB200 superchip* (two GPUs), while H100's 989 TFLOPS and 3.35 TB/s are per GPU. A reader can easily infer that a GB200 GPU has 16 TB/s of HBM3e (it does not; B200 has 8 TB/s per GPU) and that GB200 has 4,500 TFLOPS per GPU (it does not; 2,250 per GPU). The '4.8× bandwidth advantage' and '4.5× compute advantage' are likewise superchip-vs-GPU comparisons presented as if they were like-for-like.
evidence: B200 dense BF16 = 2,250 TFLOPS/GPU and 8 TB/s HBM3e/GPU; GB200 superchip = 2 GPUs → 4,500 TFLOPS and 16 TB/s. The ridge ratio is granularity-invariant (4,500/16 = 281.25 either way), so only the labelling is at issue.
root_cause: Per-part and per-GPU figures were mixed in a hardware-comparison sentence without a granularity marker.
correction: Add the granularity: 'GB200 superchip (2 GPUs): 4,500 TFLOPS dense BF16 and 16 TB/s HBM3e → 281 FLOP/byte; equivalently per GPU, 2,250 TFLOPS ÷ 8 TB/s = 281 FLOP/byte — the ridge is granularity-invariant.' Restate the advantage factors as per-GPU (2.28× compute, 2.39× bandwidth) or as superchip-vs-GPU with the basis named.
acceptance_test: Every hardware figure in the ridge comparison carries its granularity (per GPU / per superchip), and no reader can infer a per-GPU HBM bandwidth or peak that the part does not have.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph following the three-case host table
quoted_clause: 19 / 21 / 22 — and 32 (KV-only) / 34 (case (ii)) at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy, Ch 16/17 (the ρ = 1 u-only screen reads 30 / 33)
observed: The utilization-only screen is not reproducible from the stated policy: ⌈21/0.70⌉ = 30 and ⌈22/0.70⌉ = 32, not 33. The 33 is only reachable if the N−1 spare is added to the 22-host case but not to the 21-host case (⌈22/0.7⌉ + 1 = 33 versus ⌈21/0.7⌉ = 30), which is an asymmetric application of the same policy. The 32/34 pair at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy is internally consistent (⌈21/0.665⌉ + 1 = 32; ⌈22/0.665⌉ + 1 = 34), so the 'u-only' pair appears to be a different policy applied without being stated.
root_cause: A third screen variant was introduced without its policy being stated, and the arithmetic was not re-derived after the policy changed.
correction: State the u-only policy explicitly (e.g. 'utilization-only, no availability derate, no N−1 spare') and recompute, or correct the pair to 30 / 32. Verify against Ch 16/17, which own these screens.
acceptance_test: Each host-count pair in the sentence is reproducible from a stated policy (utilization derate, availability derate, N−1) and matches the corresponding table in Ch 16/17.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3 'Decode: bandwidth-bound at low batch' (KV-read caveat); compare Ch 7 §3 and Ch 7 §4
quoted_clause: Including it, the decode intensity is (140·B)/(140 + 24·B) FLOP/byte, which *saturates* at ~5.8 FLOP/byte as B→∞
observed: The symbol B is used here for batch size, while B is used for bytes-per-element in the KV formulas that this book uses throughout (Ch 7 §3: 'KV cache per token = n_layers × 2 × d_model × bytes'; Ch 7 §4: '2 × n_layers × d_hidden × bytes-per-value'; Ch 7's GQA formula '2 × n_layers × n_KV-heads × d_head × B'). The same letter carries two meanings in adjacent chapters within the same derivation family, and the expression '(140·B)/(140 + 24·B)' mixes a batch count with byte counts without units.
evidence: Ch 7 §3: 'KV cache per token (FP16) | 2 ×80 ×8192 ×2 B ≈ 2.62 MB' (B = bytes). Ch 8 §3: 'B→∞' (B = batch).
root_cause: Notation was reused across chapters without a global symbol registry.
correction: Rename the batch variable (e.g. n_batch or b) throughout the decode-intensity derivation, and write the expression with units: '(140 GFLOP × n_batch) / (140 GB + 24 GB × n_batch)'. Add a one-line symbol note where the KV formula is first introduced in Ch 7.
acceptance_test: No symbol denotes both bytes and batch size anywhere in the book; the decode-intensity expression carries units on every term.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph following the three-case host table
quoted_clause: ~$155,816.93/mo ≈ $24.97/1K at 21 hosts; ~$162,760.59/mo ≈ $26.08/1K at 22 — illustrative included-cost on the canonical 6.24M-req/mo basis, Ch 16
observed: The two monthly totals imply different per-host monthly costs: $155,816.93/21 = $7,419.85/host/mo versus $162,760.59/22 = $7,398.21/host/mo, a 0.29% difference. If the per-host cost basis is constant (as the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy implies), 22 hosts should cost $163,236.8, not $162,760.59. Either the per-host cost differs between the two cases (in which case the reason must be stated) or one figure is stale.
root_cause: Two cost figures were carried over from Ch 16 without re-deriving them against a common per-host basis.
correction: Re-derive both from Ch 16's per-host monthly cost and state it once ('$X/host/mo at the stated policy'), or explain the difference (e.g. the 22-host case includes a different spare/availability mix).
acceptance_test: The per-host monthly cost implied by each total is identical (or the difference is explained in the sentence), and both totals match Ch 16's table.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph after the host-count table
quoted_clause: the arithmetic intensity of a mature attention kernel sits near or above this ridge, meaning the kernel is compute-saturated rather than bandwidth-starved once the batch is large enough
